subject: environmental-science

moments.title: Carbon markets and scandals
moments.who: Kyoto Protocol mechanisms, voluntary carbon markets
moments.body: Kyoto introduces emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and Joint Implementation. The EU ETS (2005-) becomes the largest cap-and-trade system. Voluntary carbon markets grow rapidly post-2015. Investigations by The Guardian, Die Zeit and SourceMaterial (2023) find ~90% of Verra rainforest credits are likely 'phantom' — not delivering real emissions reductions.
moments.takeaway: Carbon markets, in principle a price-discovery mechanism for climate action, have struggled with measurement, verification and corporate greenwashing in practice.

now.title: Carbon markets today
now.body: EU ETS prices reached €90+/tonne in 2023, providing real abatement incentive in covered sectors. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (rules finalised at COP26 Glasgow, 2021) governs new international transfers. Voluntary markets have shrunk after credibility concerns. Carbon removal (CDR) credits — direct air capture, biochar, enhanced weathering — are emerging.
now.open_questions: Can carbon markets be made credible enough to deliver climate outcomes? Or are direct regulation and standards more reliable?

reflection: The price of carbon — what climate damage costs per tonne — has been studied for 30 years. Estimates range from $50 to $1000+ per tonne. The political price (the EU ETS price) has been a fraction of the social cost. Markets reveal more about preferences than about damages.
